history.subject: Mako Cloud
history.content:
Hi everyone,

If you need to simplify deployment effort and/or need free db and serverless resources , here is something you can try Mako-Cloud (cloud-test.makodb.com) for your projects. It is completely optional, and you are still welcome to use whatever cloud platform or tools you prefer. 

Mako is sort of an alternative to Supabase, except that it uses a simpler doc-like interface. The default option for Mako is to use RxDB in your frontend. With this setup, RxDB runs directly inside your application and synchronizes data with the cloud backend. This means you can skip deploying and maintaining your own Node.js server entirely. Your whole application can essentially just be a TypeScript/JavaScript web app, or a WASM app, with RxDB handling the local database and synchronization with Mako-Cloud. This can make deployment quite a bit simpler, especially for projects that do not need substantial custom server-side logic. You can simply deploy your app through github pages and never need to worry about running a server. 

Migrating from Supabase or other cloud databses should be fairly easy. I recently tried one from Supabase to Mako, and an agent handles it completely in a few hours (it is a pretty large database). 

Mako is still in its early-phase of development so you might encounter a lot of bugs. As a small compensation, if you use Mako-Cloud and find a bug, you can earn 1 bonus point for reporting it. The bonus point goes to the individual student who reports the bug, not to the entire team.

When reporting a bug, please include enough information for us to reproduce it, such as what you were doing, what you expected to happen, and what actually happened.

history.subject: Upcoming milestone review
history.content:
For the milestone presentation, the format is flexible. You should use whatever format you think best demonstrates your work and makes the most convincing case for your design.

If you are not sure how to structure it, here is a simple outline you can follow:

  1. Pick three core use cases. Choose the three use cases that you think are the most important for your application, and briefly explain why they matter. Other use cases are still important, but focus the presentation on the ones that best represent the core user experience.
  2. Talk briefly about your UI design process. Walk us through how the UI evolved. Did you iterate on the design? What did you change, and why? Was there anything interesting or unexpected that you learned while designing it? Spend about a minute sharing anything from this process that you think is worth discussing.
  3. Give a live demo. Demonstrate the three use cases through your actual UI. For a web application, show the website directly. For a mobile application, you can use a simulator or emulator.

Throughout the presentation, try to convince us that the interface would be friendly and intuitive for a real-world user. Don’t just show what the UI does; explain why the design makes sense from the user’s perspective.

Again, this is only a suggested structure. Feel free to organize the presentation differently if you think another format presents your work more effectively.

history.subject: Team-up request: Open-sourced Football Simulation and Management Game
history.content:
Hi everyone, I'm Jinyu Yang.

I was set to give a lightning talk next Monday, but I'm a bit worried right now because I still haven't found a teammate. I wanted to introduce my idea here first and see if anyone might be interested in working together.

My idea is to build a small open-source football management game based on RoboCup Soccer Simulator 2D (https://github.com/rcsoccersim/rcssmonitor). Instead of trying to compete with Football Manager, the main goal would be to make the match engine transparent, configurable, and testable. Players could inspect why an AI player made a certain decision, change tactics or player attributes, rerun situations, and run larger experiments to study how different parameters affect match results.

RoboCup already gives us a mature 2D football simulation, so we would not be building the physics engine from scratch. The goal is to build a basic management game with fictional players and clubs, formations and tactics, matches, transfers/contracts, and tools for inspecting and testing the simulation.

There are many possible directions depending on the team, including game development, AI/algorithms, simulation and physics, UI, databases, sports data analysis, and even 3D modeling.

If you are interested, read my slides [link below] and please reach out to me via Jinyu.Yang@stonybrook.edu 

https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/11fSHiZAL0QTkX7xRCRzJw2qkxuEQhdX97VQtJQ_z65Q/

history.subject: Free Tax Prep (VITA) Site Management System — real users, launching for the 2027 tax season
history.content:
<md>Hi everyone, I'm Hailey, the one who gave the short call-out after class.

I've spent the past couple of years working at a nonprofit that runs a VITA site (Volunteer Income Tax Assistance — the IRS program where trained volunteers file free tax returns for low-income families). I worked there through this past tax season, so I've seen the whole operation from the inside. More on the program here: https://www.irs.gov/individuals/irs-tax-volunteers

The workflow is genuinely broken. Clients hand-write the same info — name, SSN, DOB, address, income sources — up to four separate times across different intake forms, and volunteers then re-key all of it. That's roughly 8–10 minutes of pure paperwork per client, at 50+ clients a day. There's no queue, so nobody knows whether they're 3rd or 30th in line. And the quality review step, which the IRS requires before any return can be filed, is tracked on paper.

**So: a web platform that runs an entire VITA site for a tax season.**

- Four roles with real permission boundaries: client, preparer, quality reviewer, site coordinator
- Intake form with conditional logic + document upload (W-2s, IDs)
- A state machine for each return: intake → assigned → preparing → quality review → signature → filed / kicked back
- Live queue showing each client their position
- Automated IRS PDF generation (Form 13614-C, Form 14446) — I already have a working Python prototype for this piece
- Bilingual EN/中文: full i18n architecture, with the client-facing flow fully translated
- Audit logging — who accessed which record, when
- Coordinator stats view: clients served, language breakdown, volunteer load

**Why I think this is a good project**

Most of Milestone 1 is figuring out what to build. I already know — I've watched these exact problems cost people hours, every day of the season. That means we get to spend our time on architecture and engineering instead of inventing requirements.

It also hits every box on the syllabus cleanly: real accounts, real login, non-trivial scope, and a domain nobody else will be doing.

**A soft preference**:

**Mandarin or Cantonese.** The product is bilingual by design — the site I worked at serves a largely Chinese-speaking community, so i18n is a real. If you're interested in i18n as an engineering problem, that counts too.

I mentioned accounting/tax domain previous but actually don't worry about that.

What matters more than any of the above: you actually want to ship this by December, and you want to build something real for real users.

I'm currently applying for funding from the nonprofit. If it comes through, it should cover our AI tooling and API costs for the semester, so nobody's paying out of pocket for Claude Code or Cursor. (Hopefully!!

**Get in touch**

Reply here or email me at hanling.zheng@stonybrook.edu. There's a lot of talent in this class and I'd genuinely love to build this with three of you!  I'll share more about the project, front-end and back-end, in Wednesday's class!! :)</md>

history.subject: Welcome to Piazza!
history.content:
Piazza is a Q&A platform designed to get you great answers from classmates and instructors fast. We've put together this list of tips you might find handy as you get started:
  1. Ask questions! The best way to get answers is to ask questions! Ask questions on Piazza rather than emailing your teaching staff so everyone can benefit from the response (and so you can get answers from classmates who are up as late as you are).
  2. Edit questions and answers wiki-style. Think of Piazza as a Q&A wiki for your class. Every question has just a single students' answer that students can edit collectively (and a single instructors’ answer for instructors).
  3. Add a followup to comment or ask further questions. To comment on or ask further questions about a post, start a followup discussion. Mark it resolved when the issue has been addressed, and add any relevant information back into the Q&A above.
  4. Go anonymous. Shy? No problem. You can always opt to post or edit anonymously.
  5. Tag your posts. It's far more convenient to find all posts about your Homework 3 or Midterm 1 when the posts are tagged. Type a “#” before a key word to tag. Click a blue tag in a post or the question feed to filter for all posts that share that tag.
  6. Format code and equations. Adding a code snippet? Click the pre or tt button in the question editor to add pre-formatted or inline teletype text. Mathematical equation? Click the Fx button to access the LaTeX editor to build a nicely formatted equation.
  7. View and download class details and resources.
Click the Course Page button in your top bar to access the class syllabus, staff contact information, office hours details, and course resources—all in one place! Contact the Piazza Team anytime with questions or comments at team@piazza.com. We love feedback!
